Re: LD 1155, An Act to Ensure Appropriate County Government Operations Relating to the Position of Dedimus Justice
Dear Members of the State and Local Government Committee:
On behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association, we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony to the Committee in support of LD 1155. Counties throughout Maine rely on Dedimus Justices to ensure the proper administration of oaths, which are essential for a wide variety of county operations.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all 16 of Maine's counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 1155 do? This legislation aims to address the backlog and inefficiencies in appointing new Dedimus Justices for county operations. The bill seeks to update the list of Dedimus Justices, remove ineligible individuals, and improve the process to ensure that counties have the necessary personnel for administrative functions.
Discussion. Counties across Maine depend on Dedimus Justices to administer oaths, crucial functions in jails, and for a broad range of county operations. To fulfill this function, county governments have historically designated employees to undergo the process to become a Dedimus Justice, and receive an appointment to become one. However, in recent years, the appointment of Dedimus Justices has slowed to the point where county governments are no longer able to ensure that a Dedimus Justice is on staff. County sheriffs are facing similar challenges.
Without a Dedimus Justice on staff with county government, counties are forced to look elsewhere for these needed services. This has been challenging given that the current list of Dedimus Justices remains outdated, with many individuals who are no longer eligible to serve--some due to age, others are deceased, and others are incarcerated or living outside of Maine. This outdated list, which ties Dedimus Justices to their towns of residence, further complicates the process and creates unnecessary hurdles for counties that need access to Dedimus Justices.

MCCA Letter re LD 1155 April 2, 2025 Page 2
We fully support the provisions of LD 1155, which seeks to clean up the list of Dedimus Justices, remove individuals who can no longer serve, and modernize the process to ensure that counties can continue to operate efficiently.
Conclusion. We respectfully urge the Committee to support this important legislation to ensure appropriate county government operations. Thank you, and please let us know if you have questions or need additional information.
Respectfully submitted,

Stephen Gorden Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

Jean-Marie Caterina Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

Testimony of Representative Paul R. Flynn, District 63, Albion
In Support of LD 1155, An Act to Ensure Appropriate County Government Operations
Relating to the Position of Dedimus Justice

Before the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government. April 2, 2025

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and distinguished members of the State and Local
Government Committee, my name is Paul Flynn, and I represent House District 63, the Eastem Kennebec
County towns of Winslow, Albion, Unity Township and the Western Waldo County community of Freedom. I appear to you today to present legislation meant to address a significant deficiency facing county govermnent and some of our county law enforcement agencies. I present this Legislation of behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association.
We seek to address this with LD 1155. Counties throughout Maine rely on Dedimus Justices to ensure
that the proper administration of oaths are completed in a timely manner. Whether elected officials, those
approved as notaries. or new law enforcement officers, all are essential for a wide variety of county
operations.

What does LD 1155 do? This legislation aims to address the backlog and inefficiencies in appointing new

Dedimus Justices for county operations. The bill also seeks to assure an update to the list of Dedimus

Justices, remove ineligible individuals, and improve the process to ensure that counties have the necessary

personnel for administrative functions.

_

The Governor's office, which reviews and approves applications for new Dedimus Justices has imposed a
moratorium on this position. While no clear substantial reason has been presented for this action, it has
resulted in some serious challenges for many sheriffs and counties in replacing those staff who previously served in this position. Over the last number of years of the moratorium many staff holding the position have tumed over due to retirements or jobs changes.

Added to which there is no process for vetting the current list on the Secretary of State's website to assure
that infonnation is accurate and that those listed are still available, able and willing to serve the needs of counties or the general public.

While this is limited in scope it is necessary for the process of swearing in officials in county govemment.
I respectfully ask the committee to move LD l 155 forward with an affirmative report to address the
challenges facing those in County Government. Thank you.

District 63

Albion, Freedom and Winslow (Part) and the unorganized territories of; Unity Township

TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF LD 1155 "An Act to Ensure Appropriate County Government Operations Relating to the Position of Dedimus Justice"
April 2, 2025 TO: Honorable Members of the State & Local Government Committee FR: Ryan D. Pelletier, County Administrator, Aroostook County
Dear Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury & Distinguished Members of the Committee: My name is Ryan Pelletier and I serve as the County Administrator of Aroostook County. I am here today to testify in support of LD 1155, An Act to Ensure Appropriate County Government Operations Relating to the Position of Dedimus Justice. I won't take a lot of your time, except to tell you, that I did a search on Maine.Gov to find the people who are currently serving as Dedimus Justices here in Aroostook County. I, myself am one of those individuals. What I found was quite alarming. In my area of Aroostook County (the St. John Valley in northern Aroostook) there are a total of 25 individuals listed as Dedimus Justices with 15 of them either being retired or deceased. There is no accountability. Thank you for your time and consideration of this important legislation and I encourage you to support a unanimous Ought to Pass recommendation.

JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT

Testimony of Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State Department of the Secretary of State

April 2, 2025

Testifying in opposition to
L.D. 1155 "An Act to Ensure Appropriate County Government Operations Relating to the Position of
Dedimus Justice"
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on State
and Local Government, my name is Shenna Bellows, I live in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State. I am testifying in opposition to L.D. 1155.
The Division of Corporations, UCC and Commissions is the record-keeping entity for commissions in
Maine, including for Notaries Public, Marriage Officiants, and Dedimus Justices. Dedimus Justices perform a single function under Maine statute, that of swearing in various public officials. The office is currently a lifetime appointment by the Governor, but the application form is available from, and the paperwork managed by, the Notary Office within our Division.
Right now, there are 1,096 Dedimus Justices in Maine, though at this time it is unclear how many of them are really active in that role. More truly active Dedimus Justices are needed in order to spread out
their work. Under L.D. 1155, Maine would have just 48 Dedimus Justices and their work would be limited to county government and county sheriff duties and responsibilities. This would create a massive issue for the functioning of local and state government.
There are reforms needed in the area of the Dedimus Justice role. That is why my office worked to
introduce L.D. 129, which was heard recently by this Committee. The reforms proposed in that bill will be more effective and helpful than those proposed here in L.D. 1155. I encourage you to vote Ought Not To Pass on this bill.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide this testimony, and I am happy to answer any questions you may have.
